manufacturer technical characterization

records.notes: Avoid teaching temperature-to-flavor effects as universal absolutes; source material documents strain-specific exceptions.

records.claim: During mashing, malt enzymes -- primarily alpha- and beta-amylase -- break down starch; not all of it is broken all the way down into fermentable sugars, and some is instead converted into larger dextrins that ordinary brewing yeast does not ferment.

sources.type: manufacturer technical article
sources.ref: Briess Technical Services (Bies, D. & Roberts, C., 2013), 'Understanding a Malt Analysis'

sources.type: brewing encyclopedia entry
sources.ref: The Oxford Companion to Beer (Garrett Oliver, ed., 2011), entry 'alpha amylase'

records.notes: Alpha- and beta-amylase act together during mashing; their relative activity, not just overall enzyme presence, determines how much starch converts to fermentable sugar versus unfermentable dextrin.

records.claim: In a study that varied mash temperature between 65C and 80C, increasing mash temperature within that range reduced the fermentability of the resulting wort; mash thickness also affected the outcome.

sources.type: peer-reviewed journal article
sources.ref: R. Muller (1991), 'The effects of mashing temperature and mash thickness on wort carbohydrate composition', Journal of the Institute of Brewing 97(2):85-92, DOI 10.1002/j.2050-0416.1991.tb01055.x

records.notes: Only the abstract/metadata of this source were directly verified in this round; the publisher's full text was not accessible (returned HTTP 403). The claim is deliberately scoped to the exact 65-80C range and the temperature/thickness effects the abstract itself reports -- it must not be read as generic beginner mash-temperature guidance (80C is well above a typical beginner saccharification target) without a separate source that supports that broader, practical-brewing claim.

records.claim: The iodine test checks mash or wort for residual starch: a drop of iodine solution turning blue-black indicates starch is still present, while no blue-black color change indicates the starch has been converted.

sources.type: brewing encyclopedia entry
sources.ref: The Oxford Companion to Beer (Garrett Oliver, ed., 2011), entry 'iodine'

records.notes: Not promoted to 'verified' in this round: issue #337 requires an independent second suitable source for this specific claim before promotion, and only one source (The Oxford Companion to Beer, entry 'iodine') was available/verifiable in this round. Promote only after a second independent source is found and reviewed. Not referenced by the shipped mashing.fundamentals pilot content for this reason.

records.claim: Mash temperature is only one of several factors -- including mash thickness/water-to-grist ratio and the malt's own enzyme content -- that influence wort fermentability and carbohydrate composition; there is no single mash temperature that is universally correct for every recipe or desired beer outcome.

sources.type: peer-reviewed journal article
sources.ref: R. Muller (1991), 'The effects of mashing temperature and mash thickness on wort carbohydrate composition', Journal of the Institute of Brewing 97(2):85-92, DOI 10.1002/j.2050-0416.1991.tb01055.x

records.claim: Boiling wort to an active, sustained boil inactivates the malt enzymes that were active during mashing (stopping further starch conversion) and reduces the wort's microbial load carried over from the mash/lauter.

sources.type: established brewing-science technical text (Kunze, Technology Brewing and Malting, cited in a Brewers Association-hosted VLB presentation)

records.notes: Scope: 'reduces microbial load at the time of boiling', not a claim that the wort/kettle/equipment remains sterile afterward -- post-boil handling (chilling, transfer, fermenter sanitation) can still introduce contamination. No specific minimum time/temperature threshold is asserted. Wording trap: never say 'sterilizes'; never attach a specific minute count as a universal rule.

records.claim: Barley/malt contains a precursor that can form dimethyl sulfide (DMS) during wort heating; DMS itself is volatile, and a vigorous, sufficiently long boil is one important control that helps prevent DMS off-flavor in finished beer.

sources.type: Brewers Association off-flavor management resource covering DMS

records.notes: The precursor and DMS are distinct; this claim does not require the learner to identify or quantify the precursor. No universal minimum boil duration or malt-type threshold is asserted -- precursor levels vary by malt (more relevant for base malts like pilsner malt). Critical wording trap (issue #366 guardrail): never call the precursor itself 'volatile' or 'the thing driven off' -- DMS is what is volatile and driven off, the precursor is what forms it. Do not state a fixed 'X minutes removes all DMS risk' rule.

records.claim: Boiling causes wort proteins and polyphenols to coagulate and precipitate out -- the 'hot break'.

sources.type: established brewing-science technical text (Kunze, Technology Brewing and Malting, cited in a Brewers Association-hosted VLB presentation)

records.notes: Narrowed to the coagulation/precipitation phenomenon itself -- does not assert a specific haze/off-flavor/staling benefit from removing that material. Explicitly distinct from chill haze, which forms later, on cooling, from a different (colder-temperature) protein-polyphenol interaction. Wording trap: never conflate 'hot break' and 'chill haze' as the same phenomenon.

records.claim: In the first minutes after a wort reaches a rolling boil, a rising foam commonly forms and can rise fast enough to boil over the kettle if the kettle is fairly full and the brewer is not watching; briefly reducing heat, using an anti-foam aid, or staying attentive during this window is common homebrewing practice to prevent it.

sources.type: established homebrewing technical text (John Palmer, How to Brew, Chapter 7)

records.notes: An established, widely observed brewing practice, not a controlled study result -- does not claim a boil-over always happens, nor quantify a fill-level threshold. Wording trap: do not present as a guaranteed event ('will boil over'); do not imply a single fixed fill percentage is safe for every kettle geometry.

records.claim: Boiling converts (isomerizes) hop alpha acids into the more soluble iso-alpha-acids that are a major source of perceived bitterness in beer. Isomerization is time-dependent: a longer boil time for a given addition increases its bitterness contribution (utilization), but utilization approaches a practical ceiling rather than increasing without bound as boil time grows.

sources.type: peer-reviewed experimental review of hop alpha-acid isomerisation/utilisation

records.notes: Describes the direction and the general isomerization/utilization relationship only -- does not assert alpha acids contribute zero bitterness before isomerization, and does not assert or reproduce any specific numeric utilization curve or percentage (that remains modules/calculations.py's own implemented Tinseth model, out of scope for this teaching claim). Wording trap: do not say alpha acids are 'not bitter' before isomerization; do not state a specific utilization percentage or claim any one utilization model is the single, universally accepted number.

records.claim: Hop aroma and flavor come largely from volatile essential oils, which boil off the longer a hop addition remains in an active boil. An addition made late in the boil, at flameout, or during a post-boil whirlpool/hop-stand therefore generally retains more of its original aroma/flavor character, and generally reaches lower alpha-acid utilization (bitterness), than an otherwise-comparable early/full-boil addition -- though a hot, long whirlpool/hop-stand can still contribute material bitterness, not zero.

sources.type: manufacturer technical datasheet
AHA technical experiment with Bell's Brewery lab IBU measurements

records.notes: 'Generally lower' utilization, not 'zero' or 'negligible' -- a hot, long whirlpool/hop-stand can still contribute material bitterness. Does not assert an exact cutoff or any particular whirlpool temperature/duration as optimal. Wording trap: never say a late/whirlpool addition contributes 'zero' or 'negligible' bitterness; do not assert one specific 'correct' whirlpool temperature or hold time as a universal rule.

records.claim: Because bitterness contribution (favored by longer boil time, FACT-HOP-0001) and aroma/flavor retention (favored by shorter boil time, FACT-HOP-0002) move in opposite directions with boil time, brewers commonly use hop additions at more than one point in the process -- e.g. an early 'bittering' addition plus a late or whirlpool 'aroma/flavor' addition -- to pursue both independently in the same beer, rather than relying on a single addition.

sources.type: peer-reviewed experimental review of hop alpha-acid isomerisation/utilisation
manufacturer technical datasheet
AHA technical experiment with Bell's Brewery lab IBU measurements

records.notes: A synthesis/interpretation of FACT-HOP-0001/FACT-HOP-0002, not a new independently measured result -- describes a common brewing strategy, not a fixed numeric schedule (does not assert e.g. '60/20/5 minutes' as a required recipe). No independent citation beyond the two underlying facts' own sources is expected, mirroring FACT-MASH-0004's precedent. Wording trap: do not present any specific minute schedule as the correct or only pattern; do not imply single-addition recipes are wrong.

records.claim: A hop's alpha-acid percentage is the share of its weight that is alpha acids, and it indicates the hop's bittering potential; it is not the beer's IBU. The IBU contributed by a hop addition depends on how much hop is used and how it is used, including boil time and other process conditions, so an alpha-acid percentage does not map to any fixed IBU.

sources.type: reference encyclopedia entry (The Oxford Companion to Beer, 'alpha acids')
brewing textbook, web edition (John Palmer, How to Brew, ch. 5 Hops; (c) 1999-2015 John Palmer, page carries 2025 author notes; accessed 2026-09-30)

records.notes: Ingredient-side prerequisite only: alpha % is a hop property, alpha % != IBU, and use affects IBU. Deliberately does NOT carry calculated-recipe-IBU-is-an-estimate, wort vs finished-beer IBU, perceived bitterness, beer matrix, balance or recipe formulation -- those remain with Oppskriftsforstaaelse R-2/R-4. Wording traps: do not say 'alpha % is bitterness'; do not say '12% alpha = 12 IBU'; do not say higher alpha always means more IBU; no Tinseth/utilisation equation or utilisation percentages, no IBU target bands, no cohumulone, no hop variety catalogue. Source set fixed by Chief spot-check on issue #440 (2026-09-30); the BarthHaas BBC Pure Hop Pellet 2018 datasheet was not recoverable live and is intentionally not cited here. No producer source, so no commercial-interest flag applies.

records.claim: Hops age after harvest: warmth, oxygen and time degrade or change bittering compounds and aroma oils, so cold, oxygen-excluding storage slows deterioration and helps preserve brewing value.

sources.type: peer-reviewed two-year hop storage trial (Rutnik, Ocvirk & Kosir, Plants 2023, 12(4), 936)
manufacturer technical article (BarthHaas Group, 'Hops don't like to get old, either', 15 May 2024) -- commercial interest
manufacturer technical datasheet (BarthHaas Hop Pellets Type 90 TDS, approved 14 Jun 2024) -- commercial interest, supporting context only

records.notes: Direction only. Alpha-acid content can fall during storage, but this does NOT generalise to 'finished beer will always be less bitter'; aroma quality/intensity can decline; ageing rate depends on variety, form, packaging and conditions. Must not include: Hop Storage Index calculations/thresholds, degradation percentages, shelf-life months, exact storage temperatures, 'old hops make less bitter beer', 'old hops become cheesy/sweaty' (cheese clause deliberately dropped by Chief decision), 'vacuum sealing preserves hops' as a universal homebrew claim, 'oxygen ruins hops', 'all varieties age the same', 'pellets always store better than cones'. Two BarthHaas sources are commercial-interest; the claim is corroborated by the independent peer-reviewed trial. Source set fixed by Chief spot-check on issue #440 (2026-09-30).

records.claim: Cooling wort rapidly from boiling temperature down toward the yeast's intended pitching temperature reduces the time the wort spends in a temperature range where unwanted/spoilage microorganisms can grow, and is standard homebrewing practice for reducing infection risk before pitching.

sources.type: established homebrewing technical text (John Palmer, How to Brew, Chapter 7)
Brew Your Own technical article on wort chilling

records.notes: Describes a risk-reduction direction, not a guarantee -- does not claim rapid cooling guarantees zero infection risk, nor that slow cooling always causes infection, and does not assert a specific numeric cooling-rate threshold or fixed 'danger zone' temperature band as a universal rule. Distinct from FACT-BOIL-0001 (boiling reduces microbial load at the time of boiling) -- cooling is a separate, later exposure window, not a continuation of the same protection. Wording trap: do not imply cooling slowly always causes an infection; do not state a specific 'danger zone' temperature range as a universal fixed rule; do not imply this claim extends or repeats FACT-BOIL-0001's own microbial-load scope.

records.claim: As wort cools from boiling toward pitching temperature, proteins and polyphenols that were still soluble in hot wort coagulate again and precipitate -- 'cold break' -- a temperature-driven phenomenon distinct from the 'hot break' that forms during the boil itself (FACT-BOIL-0003).

sources.type: established homebrewing technical text (John Palmer, How to Brew, Chapter 7)
Brew Your Own technical article on wort chilling
Brew Your Own technical article on wort chillers

records.notes: Does not assert a specific quantity of cold break, nor a specific benefit or detriment from how much of it is carried into the fermenter -- homebrewers vary in how much they choose to leave behind in the kettle, and this claim does not take a side on that practice. Wording trap: never conflate cold break with hot break as the same phenomenon or the same temperature stage; never conflate cold break with chill haze (chill haze is a colder, later, different-mechanism phenomenon, already excluded from FACT-BOIL-0003's own scope).

records.claim: Boiling protects the wort by heat only while it is actively at or near boiling temperature (FACT-BOIL-0001); once cooling begins, any surface that will subsequently contact the wort or beer -- chiller, transfer hose/tubing, fermenter, airlock, and any tool used from this point forward -- is no longer protected by that heat, and needs to be clean and sanitized before and during use to avoid introducing spoilage organisms.

sources.type: established homebrewing technical text (John Palmer, How to Brew, Chapter 2)
Brew Your Own technical article on wort chillers

records.notes: Describes the existence and starting point of this handling boundary, not a specific sanitizer product, contact time, or procedure -- those vary by product and are explicitly out of scope (mirrors FACT-BOIL-0004's own 'no single fixed rule' boundary). Wording trap: do not imply one single specific sanitizer or contact time is required; do not imply the boil 'immunizes' downstream equipment or that this boundary is optional.

records.claim: Brewing yeast can use oxygen before or around pitching to synthesize sterols and unsaturated fatty acids needed for healthy membrane growth. Whether the brewer needs to deliberately aerate/oxygenate the wort is conditional: it depends on yeast form/state, pitch rate, wort gravity and manufacturer/process guidance. Fresh active dry yeast at normal first-pitch rates is a common explicit case where added wort aeration may be unnecessary, because the dried cells are produced with sterol/UFA reserves.

sources.type: manufacturer technical guidance (Wyeast, Oxygenation & Aeration)
manufacturer knowledge-center FAQ (Fermentis)
manufacturer technical guidance (Fermentis, best ways to improve fermentation)
manufacturer technical guidance (Lallemand, premium dry yeast)
manufacturer technical booklet (Lallemand, Yeast Nutrition)

records.notes: Describes both the biological role of oxygen and the operator-action exception. Does not prescribe a dissolved-oxygen target, aeration method or duration, and must not be taught as 'all wort must be aerated before pitching.' Wording trap: do not turn 'oxygen can support growth' into 'the brewer must always add oxygen'; do not imply oxygen is wanted throughout fermentation; keep fresh first-pitch dry yeast as an explicit common exception to mandatory aeration.

records.claim: Once fermentation is actively underway, oxygen exposure to the wort/beer is generally undesirable: it can contribute to oxidative off-flavors (e.g. cardboard/'stale' notes), diminished hop aroma, and reduced shelf stability. Minimizing splashing and unnecessary air contact during any transfer performed after active fermentation has begun is standard homebrewing practice.

sources.type: Brew Your Own technical article on racking and transferring
Brew Your Own technical article on transferring beer

records.notes: Describes a risk/quality direction, not an absolute threshold or guaranteed outcome -- does not claim a single stray oxygen exposure inevitably ruins a batch. Wording trap: do not imply any oxygen contact after pitching instantly spoils the beer; do not conflate this with the pre-pitch requirement in FACT-OXY-0001 -- same molecule, opposite-timing effect, not a contradiction.

records.claim: Practical oxygen guidance is both timing- and yeast-dependent. Before/at pitching, oxygen availability can be beneficial where the yeast/process requires it, but deliberate aeration is not universally required (fresh active dry yeast at normal first pitch is a common exception). Once fermentation is actively underway, unnecessary oxygen exposure should generally be minimized.

sources.type: manufacturer technical guidance (Wyeast, Oxygenation & Aeration)
Brew Your Own technical article on transferring beer

records.notes: A synthesis/interpretation of FACT-OXY-0001/FACT-OXY-0002, not a new independently measured result -- does not define one universal oxygen target or one exact temporal cutoff for every fermentation. Wording trap: never state this as simply 'oxygen is bad', 'oxygen is always wanted before pitching', or 'always aerate wort'; the teaching point is conditional need before pitch and minimized unnecessary oxygen once active fermentation is underway.

records.claim: Homebrewers commonly move wort/beer between vessels either by gravity (relying on an elevation difference between vessels, requiring no pump) or with a pump (works regardless of relative vessel height, at the cost of added equipment and cleaning); a closed/sealed transfer path (e.g. a hose run vessel-to-vessel with minimal open-air contact) reduces splashing and airborne contamination/oxygen exposure compared with an open pour or open racking, at the cost of added setup complexity.

sources.type: Brew Your Own technical article on transferring beer
established homebrewing technical text (John Palmer, How to Brew, Chapter 9)

records.notes: Describes the trade-off directions only -- does not claim one method is universally 'correct', does not recommend a specific pump/hose product, and does not assert a numeric contamination-rate difference between methods. Wording trap: do not present gravity or pump transfer as inherently superior; do not imply an open transfer always causes contamination, or that a closed transfer eliminates the risk.

records.claim: Adding a small, measured amount of fermentable ('priming') sugar to beer immediately before sealing it into bottles triggers a renewed, small-scale fermentation inside each sealed bottle. Because the CO2 produced by that renewed fermentation has no other escape path, it dissolves into the beer under the pressure that builds inside the sealed bottle, carbonating it. The amount of priming sugar needed depends on the specific beer (its existing dissolved CO2, temperature, style) and the carbonation level wanted -- there is no single universal number that applies to every batch.

sources.type: manufacturer technical guidance (Lallemand Brewing, Best Practices -- Bottle conditioning with CBC-1)
manufacturer brewing calculator documentation (Lallemand Brewing, Bottle conditioning calculator)
AHA technical article on bottle conditioning

records.notes: States the mechanism and the 'no universal number' boundary only -- does not provide or endorse a specific priming-sugar dosage, formula, or table, and does not name a specific priming-sugar type/product. Wording trap: do not state a specific priming-sugar amount/table as correct or required; do not imply any fermentable sugar type works identically; do not imply this is the same mechanism as the original fermentation rather than a distinct, smaller, sealed-container renewal of it.

records.claim: Beer can also be carbonated in a sealed keg by connecting it to an external CO2 supply under pressure, with no renewed/secondary fermentation involved. The amount of CO2 that ends up dissolved in the beer depends on the pressure applied, the beer's temperature, and the time/contact method used (e.g. a slower 'set and forget' equilibrium approach versus a faster agitation-based approach) -- carbonation level is directly adjustable by the brewer rather than fixed by however much priming sugar was added.

sources.type: AHA technical article on kegging homebrew
Brewers Association technical resource on draught beer carbonation
manufacturer technical guidance (Lallemand Brewing, Preserving thiols in homebrewing)

records.notes: Describes the concept and the governing variables (pressure, temperature, time) only -- does not provide a specific pressure/temperature/time schedule or carbonation-level target, and does not compare or recommend specific CO2 regulator/keg equipment brands or models. Wording trap: do not present one specific pressure/temperature/time combination as 'the' carbonation schedule; do not name or favor a specific keg/regulator brand; do not imply force carbonation is strictly faster or better than bottle conditioning -- it is a different mechanism with different trade-offs, not a superior one (see FACT-PACK-0004).

records.claim: Whichever packaging path is used, the beer ends up sealed inside a container that is actively carbonating (bottle conditioning) or being force-carbonated (keg) -- meaning that container holds internal pressure. Using a package, vessel or fitting that is damaged or not intended/rated for the pressure involved creates a risk of over-pressure, leakage or container/equipment failure. Brewers should use pressure-suitable packaging/equipment and respect its rated operating limits.

sources.type: Brewers Association educational publication on package over-pressurization
manufacturer technical guidance (Lallemand Brewing, Preserving thiols in homebrewing)
established homebrewing technical text (John Palmer, How to Brew, Chapter 11)

records.notes: States the existence of this safety boundary and its general cause (unsuitable container/fitting under pressure), not a specific pressure rating, a specific safe/unsafe product list, or a full pressure-vessel engineering treatment. Wording trap: do not name a specific unsafe or safe product/brand; do not turn this into pressure numbers, burst-pressure ratings, or a design/engineering lesson; do not imply every packaging attempt is dangerous -- the point is container/equipment suitability, not that pressure itself is inherently hazardous when suitable equipment is used correctly.

records.claim: Bottling and kegging are both legitimate, widely used homebrewing packaging methods -- neither is a marker of a 'better' or more serious brewer, and the appropriate choice for a given brewer depends on practical factors (equipment cost/availability, storage space, how quickly the beer will be served, personal preference), not on any inherent quality difference in the resulting beer. Once the sanitation boundary (FACT-COOL-0003) has been respected and the beer has been properly primed/conditioned or force-carbonated (FACT-PACK-0001/FACT-PACK-0002) and given appropriate time, either path reaches the same natural completion point: a carbonated, conditioned beer ready to serve or store.

records.notes: A synthesis/interpretation drawing on FACT-PACK-0001/FACT-PACK-0002/FACT-PACK-0003 and reused FACT-COOL-0003/FACT-OXY-0002, not a new independently measured result. Does not claim every homebrewer's context makes both methods equally convenient in practice -- only that neither is inherently a 'better beer' marker. Wording trap: never present bottling as 'the beginner method' and kegging as 'the real/serious brewer method,' or vice versa; never imply a brewer must eventually 'graduate' from one to the other; keep the 'natural completion point' framing as an end to the process, not a claim that packaging is the end of the brewer's learning journey.

records.claim: In Brew In A Bag (BIAB), the full grain bill is mashed while contained inside a porous bag placed directly in the same kettle/mash vessel used for the rest of the brew day. Instead of draining wort through a separate lauter tun or false bottom, wort/grain separation happens by lifting the bag out of the kettle (commonly allowing it to drain, and sometimes followed by a simple dunk in additional hot water) -- functionally combining the mash and separation steps into fewer vessels than the traditional layout in FACT-METHOD-0002.

sources.type: American Homebrewers Association technical guide, Brew in a Bag (BIAB)
American Homebrewers Association technical article, Homebrew Equipment

records.notes: Describes the mechanism only -- does not assert BIAB always omits a separate sparge/rinse step (some BIAB brewers do dunk-sparge the bag), and does not assert BIAB is more or less efficient than traditional all-grain (no numeric efficiency claim). Does not name a specific bag material, size or brand. Wording trap: never call BIAB 'not real all-grain brewing' -- the same whole-grain mash/conversion chemistry applies (FACT-MASH-0001); never imply BIAB requires specialized equipment beyond a bag and a kettle; never state BIAB is universally more or less efficient than the other two methods.

records.claim: In traditional separate-vessel all-grain brewing, mashing takes place in a dedicated mash/lauter vessel -- often using a false bottom, braided-hose manifold, or similar filter medium to form a 'grain bed' -- and the resulting wort is drained into a separate brewing kettle, typically with an additional sparge step rinsing the grain bed with more hot water to recover further sugar. Using a dedicated mash/lauter vessel is a matter of equipment/process layout, not a separate underlying brewing chemistry from BIAB (FACT-METHOD-0001) or an all-in-one system (FACT-METHOD-0003).

Wording trap: never imply the mash chemistry itself differs from BIAB's -- same starch-conversion process (FACT-MASH-0001); never present traditional all-grain as the 'proper' or 'real' method relative to the other two.

records.claim: An all-in-one brewing system integrates mashing and boiling -- and often wort recirculation and/or built-in heating/temperature control -- into a single vessel, commonly using an internal perforated basket, malt pipe, or similar filter element to hold the grain bed for mashing and enable wort/grain separation within that same vessel, rather than requiring the brewer to physically move wort between separate mash and boil vessels. Recirculating the wort through the grain bed (where present) and electric heating/temperature control change how a brewer manages the process without changing the underlying mash/boil chemistry already described in FACT-MASH-0001/FACT-BOIL-0001.

records.claim: Regardless of which method context is used, the water volumes, dead space, grain handling, and recirculation/sparging approach a brewer needs to plan for can differ meaningfully by equipment/method -- for example, a bag-based system's absorption/retention characteristics and a false-bottom or malt-pipe system's dead space are not identical -- so a recipe's practical water/time planning should account for the brewer's own equipment rather than assuming one universal set of numbers works identically across BIAB, traditional all-grain, and all-in-one systems.

records.claim: BIAB, traditional separate-vessel all-grain, and all-in-one brewing machines are all legitimate, widely used all-grain homebrewing approaches that share the same underlying mash/boil/cool/ferment/package process (FACT-MASH-0001, FACT-BOIL-0001). The appropriate choice for a given brewer depends on contextual factors -- available equipment, space, budget, batch size, and workflow preference -- not on any one method being inherently a 'better,' more advanced, or more 'real' brewing method than the others.

records.claim: Malted barley is a basic brewing ingredient that supplies the carbohydrates/sugars for fermentation as well as colour and flavour. Barley is well suited to malting because of its husk, its starch reserve and its enzyme system. Malting is a sequence of steeping, germination and drying: germination opens up the grain's starch reserves, and drying halts growth so that the starch remains available to the brewer.

sources.type: producer technical material
sources.ref: Briess, 'The Malting Process' (Brewing with Briess, Malting 101), https://brewingwithbriess.com/malting-101/malting-process/

records.claim: Brewing malts are commonly divided into base (standard/brewers) malts and specialty malts. Base malts contain high enzyme levels together with the carbohydrates/sugars needed for fermentation. Specialty malts are produced by altering the malting/drying conditions to develop flavour, colour or other function; more intense heating reduces the enzymes available, and many specialty malts are designed to be used at smaller inclusion levels.

sources.type: producer technical material
sources.ref: Briess, 'The Malting Process' (Brewing with Briess, Malting 101), https://brewingwithbriess.com/malting-101/malting-process/

records.notes: Single-source (Briess) producer technical claim, Tier A. Wording trap: say 'many specialty malts', never 'all'; never state that specialty malt has no enzymes or can never self-convert, and never state that base malt is always the largest part of a grist; no temperature/time numbers, no named malt products or catalogue recommendations. Enzyme role in mashing stays with FACT-MASH-0001/FACT-MASH-0004.

records.claim: The conditions used when specialty malts are dried, kilned or roasted develop different colour and flavour characteristics, and malt colour materially affects the colour of the finished beer, so a recipe may need adjusting to hit a colour target. Thermal processing of specialty malt involves non-enzymatic browning (caramelisation, pyrolysis and Maillard reactions) that contributes aroma compounds, and time, temperature and moisture during that processing materially influence flavour development. The relation between malt colour and aroma/flavour is complex, so colour is not a direct one-to-one predictor of flavour.

It is NOT chemistry truth, a measurement, a quality score, a numeric target or a style score. Generic wording only ('the different parts of a beer'); NOT a component list. Balance is not quality: never teach balanced = better or unbalanced = flawed; intentional dominance can be valid. Style is optional context only: never inside BJCP range = balanced or outside range = unbalanced; BJCP is context, not sensory science. BU:GU is an App/Master-view heuristic only -- NOT a Course Fact, learning objective, quiz target, sensory measurement or universal balance score; no BU:GU thresholds or bands appear here; same BU:GU may correspond to different perceived balance. NO directional component claims for alcohol, residual sugar/FG, roast, water minerals, carbonation, pH, temperature, hop aroma/flavour or acidity (no 'more sweetness requires more IBU', 'more alcohol requires more IBU', 'high FG needs more hops', 'roast needs X bitterness'). records.claim: Gravity (also called specific gravity, formally relative density) is the density of wort or beer relative to water, compared at stated reference temperatures. Dissolved sugar raises it, and it generally falls during fermentation as yeast turns sugar into alcohol. Original gravity (OG) is the gravity measured before fermentation begins, and final gravity (FG) is the gravity measured when fermentation has finished.
